title: The G20 under Trump: The impact of a leaner agenda
author: Abhinandan Kumar
text: |G20, explained.A leaner G20 is not inherently a bad idea (US Department of State)The G20 under Trump: The impact of a leaner agenda Almost a year into US leadership, objections from China and disagreement with South Africa are among various barriers to outcomes. Abhinandan Kumar4 November 20264 min read|The G20 under Trump: The impact of a leaner agenda The G20 under Trump: The impact of a leaner agenda When the United States assumed the 2026 Presidency of the Group of 20 (G20) in December 2025, it promised to return the forum to its “core mission” (Opens in new window) of economic growth and prosperity. Its priorities (Opens in new window) centred around four working groups focused on reducing regulatory burdens, securing affordable energy, advancing technological innovation, and promoting fair, reciprocal, and balanced trade. Almost 11 months later, the record suggests that Washington has secured some tangible outcomes, but it is less clear whether its narrower approach has made international economic cooperation more effective.A leaner G20 is not inherently a bad idea. Under successive Global South leadership cycles in recent years, the forum's agenda expanded to encompass development finance, climate action, digital governance, health regime, food security, and reform of international institutions. These issues are no doubt important, but their accumulation also raises questions about whether the G20 is becoming what it sought to replace (Opens in new window). A forum that attempts to address almost every global challenge risks diluting its attention.So, has a narrower agenda delivered in 2026? The strongest evidence of progress comes from the energy track. At the September 2026 G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial in Houston, Texas, G20 Energy Ministers reached consensus on four outcomes (Opens in new window) covering household energy access, regulatory efficiency for infrastructure development, water resilience, and critical mineral supply chains. The G20 Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill, North Carolina produced a statement in the form of the Carolina Principles (Opens in new window) for Emerging Technologies, alongside initiatives on Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption, workforce development, and technology-related intellectual property.The G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors meeting provided a more complicated picture. Following its September meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, the Chair's Statement (Opens in new window) welcomed the streamlining of the track's structure and agenda that highlighted productivity, global imbalances, sovereign debt, financial literacy, digital assets, and financial sector regulation. However, the statement also records China's objection to several paragraphs, including those on global economic risks and imbalances.While seeking national benefits from its G20 presidency is not wrong, what stands out is the explicit positioning of those benefits as the core purpose of hosting a forum whose legitimacy rests on cooperation among its members.Similarly, at the G20 Trade Ministerial (Opens in new window) in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, members agreed on condemning the weaponisation of food through coercive trade measures. They did not, however, reach consensus on the proposed statement on forced labour in supply chains, while a US-backed proposal on structural excess capacity also failed to secure agreement. Ministers also expressed differing views on reforming the Most-Favoured-Nation principle.These disagreements show that narrowing the range of issues under discussion does not remove the underlying conflicts that constrain collective action, and that fewer priorities do not necessarily produce greater consensus.Besides the narrowing of the agenda, the way President Donald Trump’s administration has pursued this reorientation raises a different set of concerns. The starkest example has been the exclusion of South Africa from the 2026 proceedings. In November 2025, Trump announced (Opens in new window) that South Africa would not be invited to participate in the US-hosted G20 meetings, citing what he described as the South African government's mistreatment of white Afrikaners and its alleged human rights violations.Trump also objected to South Africa's handover of the G20 presidency following the Johannesburg summit, which the US had boycotted. South African President Cyril Ramaphosa subsequently reaffirmed (Opens in new window) that South Africa remained a founding member of the forum and intended to continue participating as a full member.While a presidency can propose fewer priorities and seek agreement on issues that deserve collective attention, excluding a member is a different exercise. It creates a tension between the US objective of making the G20 more focused and the principle of inclusive cooperation that lies at the heart of the forum. Moreover, its implications extend to the G20's institutional continuity. Under the established troika arrangement, the previous, current, and incoming presidencies work together to maintain continuity across successive years. Dispensing with the troika by excluding the previous host risks making the G20 more dependent on the preferences of the incumbent presidency.Trump’s unilateralism vis-a-vis the G20 can be understood in the context of his broader approach to multilateralism. Since returning to office for a second term, he has withdrawn the US from several international institutions and agreements, including the World Health Organisation, and in January 2026 directed its withdrawal (Opens in new window) from 66 international organisations and bodies.As analysts have noted (Opens in new window), Trump’s approach combines withdrawal and disruption with selective engagement in institutions that serve his administration's priorities. The G20 perfectly illustrates this pattern. One of the core missions stated on the home page (Opens in new window) of the official G20 presidency website is “strengthening partnerships that benefit American workers, businesses, and allies.” While seeking national benefits from its G20 presidency is not wrong, what stands out is the explicit positioning of those benefits as the core purpose of hosting a forum whose legitimacy rests on cooperation among its members.The Miami Leaders' Summit on 14-15 December will provide a final opportunity to assess the US presidency, but the record over the preceding 11 months already offers grounds for a preliminary judgement. The case for a leaner G20 remains defensible. But efficiency is not an end in itself. There is a distinction between narrowing the G20’s priorities through collective deliberation, and reshaping the forum through unilateral decisions. A more focused agenda can strengthen the G20 – only if it preserves the participation, consultation, and continuity necessary for collective action.About the authorAbhinandan KumarAbhinandan Kumar is a PhD Candidate at the Department of International Relations, Jadavpur University.TopicsG20Donald TrumpUnited StatesThe Interpreter on G20Explore The InterpreterDiplomacyThe minilateral moment is passing29 June 2026Abhinandan KumarDiplomacyWho speaks for the Global South?4 May 2026Sanchari GhoshEconomyHigh rates and expensive oil create a global debt trap10 April 2026Nischal DhungelMore on G20Explore G20Research (Opens in new window)China versus America on global tradeData Snapshot by Roland Rajah, Ahmed AlbayrakResearchThe case for an Indo-Pacific Economic Resilience BankAnalysis by Michelle Lyons, Roland Rajah + 1 otherConversationsJeffrey Sachs on global cooperation and sustainable development in the time of COVID-19Alexandre DayantResearchSubmission to the Joint Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Inquiry into the Implications of the COVID-19 Pandemic for Australia's Foreign Affairs, Defence and TradeSubmission by Michael Fullilove, Stephen Grenville + 15 others
